superficial

soo-per-FISH-ul — contains 'surface'; something superficial stays right on the surface. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Superficial is existing or occurring on the surface; lacking depth or thoroughness.

The doctor reassured the family that the cut was only superficial and would heal within a few days without stitches.

Worked Example

A student writes a book report that lists the title, the author, and the number of pages, but never once mentions what the story was actually about or why it mattered to the main character.

Covering only the outer facts without ever digging into what's underneath is exactly what superficial means. Unlike 'brief,' which just means short, superficial specifically means shallow, lacking real depth.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cursory: Cursory describes the manner of the work: done quickly, with only a passing glance at the details. Superficial judges the result: it never gets beneath the surface. A careful, unhurried report can still be superficial if it only repeats the obvious facts.

surface-level: Surface-level literally names where something stays — on the outside, the visible part — and it is fairly neutral about it. Superficial says the same thing as a criticism: staying on the surface when depth was needed and expected.

skin-deep: Skin-deep means only as deep as the outer layer, and it usually describes qualities like beauty or charm that have nothing underneath. Superficial applies far more widely: analysis, friendships, knowledge — even a doctor's description of a minor cut.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

thorough: complete and carried out with great attention to detail

profound: very deep or great; showing deep understanding

Where it sits · how little depth it has — brief → superficial → shallow

brief vs. superficial: Brief is weaker than superficial — something brief is just short, while something superficial is specifically shallow, skipping over what actually matters.

shallow vs. superficial: Shallow can feel even more critical than superficial in some contexts: both mean lacking depth, but shallow more often criticizes a person's character, not just their work.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — super-

Prefix — super-: above, over (Latin)

Root — -fici-

Root — -fici-: face, surface (from Latin facies, 'face'; the a becomes i inside compound words)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin superficies combined super- ('above, over') with facies ('face, surface'): super- + fici (the compound form of facies) + -al ('relating to') -- 'the outer face of something.' Something superficial relates only to that outer surface, never what's underneath.

Use the root in a new word: surface

Use the root in a new word: surface: Rainwater collected on the surface of the old stone patio.
